conditions.name: Allergic rhinitis

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: An allergic reaction in the nose. Sneezing fits, clear runny nose and itchy watery eyes, recurring in a season or around a specific trigger, and never with fever.
workup: Skin prick or specific IgE testing if unclear

exam.step: Test visual acuity in each eye
exam.positive: Normal acuity is essential to this diagnosis
Round, reactive and equal
Follicles or papillae; excludes a foreign body
No corneal uptake

labs.confirms: Normal vision and a normal pupil are the key checks

labs.test: Swab only if severe, neonatal or gonococcal suspected

conditions.name: Conjunctivitis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Inflammation of the surface membrane of the eye. Redness with discharge and grittiness but normal vision and a normal pupil, which is what separates it from serious causes.
workup: Refer if vision affected or pupil abnormal

exam.positive: Ptosis, miosis, lacrimation and rhinorrhoea on the painful side
Pacing, unlike the stillness of migraine

labs.confirms: Excludes a secondary cause at first presentation

conditions.name: Cluster headache

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Book an appointment in the next few days

conditions.summary: Excruciating pain around one eye lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, with a red watering eye and blocked nostril on the same side. Patients pace rather than lie still.

exam.positive: Circumcorneal injection, deepest at the limbus
Small, irregular and poorly reactive
Pain in the affected eye when light is shone in the other

labs.confirms: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber

conditions.name: Anterior uveitis (iritis)
conditions.summary: Inflammation inside the front of the eye. A deep aching red eye with marked light sensitivity, a small irregular pupil and blurred vision, often recurrent.

exam.positive: Mid-dilated and unreactive

exam.step: Palpate the globe gently through the closed lid
exam.positive: Stony hard compared with the other eye
Markedly reduced with haloes
A cloudy oedematous cornea

labs.test: Test acuity and palpate the globe
labs.confirms: A stony-hard globe with reduced acuity confirms at the bedside

conditions.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

conditions.summary: Drainage of the eye blocks abruptly and pressure soars. A rock-hard painful red eye with halos, an oval fixed pupil and vomiting. Sight is lost within hours.

exam.positive: Painful or restricted movement distinguishes from preseptal

exam.step: Test visual acuity and colour vision
exam.positive: Reduction indicates optic nerve compromise
Forward displacement of the globe

exam.step: Test for relative afferent pupillary defect
exam.positive: Indicates optic nerve involvement

labs.test: Test eye movements, acuity and colour vision
labs.confirms: Painful restricted movement separates it from preseptal cellulitis

labs.test: CT orbits and sinuses with contrast
labs.confirms: Defines the abscess and sinus source

conditions.name: Orbital cellulitis

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

conditions.summary: Infection behind the eye, usually spreading from the sinuses. The lid swells shut, the eye bulges and hurts to move, with fever. Threatens sight and can spread to the brain.
workup: Check colour vision and eye movements

exam.positive: Usually looks relatively normal or mildly injected -- a clinical diagnosis from symptoms more than dramatic signs
Significant pain, photophobia, or reduced vision suggest corneal involvement needing urgent review

labs.test: Schirmer's test or ocular surface staining

conditions.name: Dry eye syndrome

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Gritty, burning, or foreign-body sensation in the eyes, sometimes with paradoxical watering, worse with screen use, wind, or air conditioning; more common with age and in dry/dusty climates. Rising with increased screen time and urban air pollution/dust exposure. Significant pain, photophobia, or reduced vision suggest a more serious ocular surface problem needing urgent ophthalmology review.
workup: Schirmer's test or ocular surface staining in specialist settings if diagnosis unclear
Punctal plugs or anti-inflammatory drops for more severe/chronic cases

exam.step: Inspect the eyelid margins for redness, crusting/scale at the lash base, and telangiectasia
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark findings distinguishing blepharitis from other causes of red eye

exam.step: Ask specifically about the CHRONICITY and RECURRING pattern of symptoms, and the ABSENCE of thick pus-like discharge
exam.positive: Blepharitis is characteristically chronic/relapsing and non-purulent -- thick pus should prompt considering bacterial conjunctivitis instead

exam.step: Ask about contact lens use and any recent contact with someone with 'pink eye'
exam.positive: Blepharitis is NOT typically contagious, unlike infective conjunctivitis -- a genuine distinguishing point for reassurance

labs.test: Clinical examination of the lid margins
labs.confirms: Usually sufficient for diagnosis -- laboratory testing is rarely needed

labs.test: Referral to ophthalmology if not responding to standard lid hygiene, or if vision is affected
labs.confirms: For more resistant or atypical cases

conditions.name: Blepharitis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins, causing redness, itching, a gritty foreign-body sensation and crusting at the base of the eyelashes -- typically relapsing-remitting rather than a single acute infection. Distinct from Conjunctivitis sharing this bundle: blepharitis is a chronic, non-contagious eyelid-margin condition (not spread by contact), and does NOT typically produce the purulent (pus-like) discharge seen in bacterial conjunctivitis.
workup: Warm compresses and gentle eyelid margin hygiene (diluted baby shampoo or a proprietary lid scrub) twice daily -- the mainstay of management
Screen for an underlying cause (seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea, or meibomian gland dysfunction, a closely related eyelid-margin/tear-film condition)
Topical antibiotic or short-course topical steroid for flares not responding to hygiene alone, under medical guidance
Address associated dry eye symptoms, which are genuinely common alongside blepharitis

exam.step: Confirm the finding is a sharply demarcated red patch with entirely normal vision and NO pain
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark -- painless, vision-unaffected, sharply demarcated redness is very characteristic and reassuring

exam.step: Ask about triggers (coughing, straining, vomiting, anticoagulant use) and check blood pressure
exam.positive: Identifies a genuine, addressable underlying cause, particularly for recurrent cases

exam.step: Screen for pain, photophobia or blurred vision, looking for their ABSENCE
exam.positive: Their presence would suggest a different, more serious cause (uveitis, glaucoma, orbital cellulitis) rather than simple subconjunctival haemorrhage

labs.confirms: Usually entirely sufficient for diagnosis -- no investigation is needed for a single, typical, painless episode

labs.test: Blood pressure check; clotting screen if recurrent
labs.confirms: For recurrent or unexplained cases, to look for an underlying treatable cause

conditions.name: Subconjunctival haemorrhage
aka: Burst blood vessel in the eye

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: A sharply demarcated, bright-red patch on the white of the eye caused by a small burst blood vessel under the conjunctiva -- dramatic-looking but genuinely benign and, critically, PAINLESS with entirely normal vision. This painless, vision-unaffected pattern is the single most important distinguishing feature from every other condition in this bundle (Uveitis, Acute Glaucoma, Orbital Cellulitis, Conjunctivitis), all of which involve genuine pain and/or visual disturbance -- their presence should prompt reconsidering one of those instead.
workup: Reassurance -- this is a benign, self-limiting condition that resolves on its own over 1-2 weeks as the blood is reabsorbed, without treatment
Ask about triggers: forceful coughing, sneezing, straining, vomiting, eye rubbing, or anticoagulant/antiplatelet medication use
Check blood pressure, particularly if recurrent -- uncontrolled hypertension is a genuine, treatable underlying association
Investigate for a bleeding/clotting disorder if recurrent without an obvious trigger, or if bruising elsewhere is also present

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Painful red eye with visual change
redFlags.message: A painful red eye with halos around lights, an odd-looking pupil or reduced vision can mean pressure inside the eye has risen dangerously.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now. Sight can be lost within hours.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Swelling around the eye with fever
redFlags.message: Swelling around the eye with fever and pain on moving the eye can mean infection behind the eye, which can spread to the brain.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
